answers.question: What is Doyon's delivered cost of coal and oil per MWh at Fort Wainwright, and does the privatisation contract allow new generation to be added to the rate base?
answers.finding: No RCA filing or company document found publishes a $/MWh or $/MMBtu delivered cost for Fort Wainwright's coal and oil generation; Doyon's own tariffs page lists only a Fort Wainwright wastewater tariff, and current RCA rate-case notices disclose aggregate revenue requirements, not per-unit rates. The contract does operate as cost-of-service rate-base regulation: in a 2011-2012 dispute Doyon said it was losing $1.1 million a month at Fort Wainwright, Fort Greely and Fort Richardson combined, after claiming $79 million of plant additions in its rate base that the government called inaccurate, which shows the rate base does absorb new capital additions (Doyon separately added a 2 MW oil-fired generator at Fort Wainwright's coal plant in 2009) but that specific additions are contested case by case rather than automatically approved. Separately, Fort Wainwright was excluded from the Army's Janus program: the August 26, 2026 selection named five vendor-installation pairs (Fort Bragg, Fort Campbell, Fort Hood, Fort Benning, Fort Drum), and Fort Wainwright was not one of them, so it remains an unmatched Janus candidate as of this research.

answers.question: Why did the board table it: cost, vendor risk or something else in the cached release? And is the cooperative open to re-running the study with a different vendor?
answers.finding: CVEA's own account (the August 9, 2023 release, reprinted in Ruralite's September 2023 issue) says the board tabled the project on economics, not vendor risk: after the fall-2022 feasibility study, CVEA's internal economic analysis found the project technically feasible but concluded there was too much economic risk for the members to own and operate it themselves, so CVEA instead pursued a power purchase agreement with USNC as owner-operator. USNC then determined in July 2023 that a PPA meeting CVEA's needs would require additional year-round heat and/or power customers to be economically feasible, and without that PPA CVEA said it could no longer pursue the project. The release explicitly leaves the door open, stating the co-op will continue to monitor the technology and may reassess if economic conditions improve, and outgoing CEO Travis Million said the MMR technology may not be the solution today but could still be in the future. The same document shows CVEA was already vendor-agnostic before choosing USNC: it names Westinghouse, Oklo, NuScale and Radiant Technologies as other MMR manufacturers it was in conversations with, and picked USNC because the projected unit size best matched CVEA's system, not out of exclusivity. No CVEA statement since USNC's October 2024 Chapter 11 filing was found reacting to it or naming a prospective replacement vendor.

answers.question: What does Teck pay per delivered gallon and per MWh today, and would NANA, as landowner, take an ownership stake in a relocatable unit?
answers.finding: Neither figure is publicly disclosed: no $/gallon or $/MWh cost for Red Dog's diesel generation appears in any Teck filing, sustainability report or news account found, and a Teck spokesperson explicitly declined to give a cost estimate when reporters asked about the mine's planned solar project (reported March 2026). What is confirmed is scale and structure: Red Dog burns roughly 40,000 gallons of diesel each day, and the mine's plan to displace some of that diesel is a solar-plus-battery project that Tugliq Energy, a Canadian company, would build and operate, selling the power back to Teck under a negotiated power purchase agreement, on a 30-acre site partly on land owned by NANA. That build-own-operate-and-sell-power structure is the closest existing precedent for how a reactor deal at Red Dog would likely be structured. NANA's own 'Future of Red Dog Mine' page, which focuses entirely on permitting the Aktigiruq/Anarraaq extension before the current Aqqaluk ore deposit is exhausted, makes no mention of energy generation, ownership stakes in power assets, or nuclear technology, and no public NANA statement on taking an ownership position in generation of any kind was found anywhere.

figures.red_dog_solar_deal_structure: Tugliq Energy builds and operates the solar-plus-battery project; Teck buys the power under a negotiated PPA

answers.question: Which Nunavut communities draw more than 1 MW year-round, and has the territory taken a position on nuclear under its own energy strategy?
answers.finding: QEC's installed-capacity data, as tabulated by community on Wikipedia's list of Nunavut generating stations (the per-community figures are not fetched from a QEC page here), shows 19 of Nunavut's 25 diesel plants exceed 1 MW of installed capacity: Iqaluit leads at 13.6 MW, followed by Rankin Inlet (3.55 MW) and Cambridge Bay (3.11 MW), down to Sanikiluaq at 1.2 MW; only six communities (Chesterfield Inlet, Grise Fiord, Kimmirut, Kugaaruk, Naujaat, Whale Cove) sit below 1 MW. QEC's fleet totals approximately 76,000 kilowatts of installed diesel capacity across all 25 communities. On the nuclear question, QEC's own 2023-2026 Corporate Plan devotes a full section to alternative energy that discusses solar PV, battery storage, geothermal and district heating at length and does not mention nuclear power, small modular reactors, or microreactors anywhere; its stated constraint is that its small customer base and the cost of its generation projects limit its financial ability to pursue new energy studies on its own, so it depends on federal partnership funding rather than any in-house generation-technology roadmap. A separate web listing suggests QEC is formally named as a participant in Canada's SMR Action Plan in a research-only, wait-and-see capacity, but the source page could not be fetched (repeated certificate errors), so that specific claim is reported here only as an unverified lead, not a finding.

answers.question: Is Nukik open to a generation asset in place of or alongside the line, and what is Agnico's diesel contract price?
answers.finding: Nukik's own framework leaves room for a generation asset, not just the transmission line: its memorandum of understanding with Qulliq Energy Corporation commits both parties to a Kivalliq Regional Energy Plan that explicitly weighs local renewable energy generation alongside the potential role of transmission in the region, evaluated by an independent planner in the best interest of electricity users -- language that treats on-site generation and the transmission line as parallel options rather than ranking the line first. No Nukik statement was found that names nuclear specifically among those generation options. On cost, Agnico's Meliadine mine, the Kivalliq region's largest diesel load, runs a 31.3 MW diesel-fuelled generation facility built from six 5.2 MW units, but no source found discloses Agnico's $/litre or $/MWh diesel contract price at Meliadine or elsewhere in the Kivalliq region; it does not appear in Agnico's own press materials on the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link or in trade coverage of the project.
